survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note is a governance and expenditure overview of Austria’s adult skills system and does not analyze student-level ILSA microdata. As a result, there is no sampling frame, no plausible-value (PV) scaling, and no survey-weight or replicate-weight variables to apply. The tables describe institutional responsibilities and expenditure shares across governance levels (federal, regional, local), not statistical estimation from a complex survey. If analysts were to conduct an ILSA-based empirical study on adult skills outcomes, they would need to use the relevant ILSA-provided sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) for population-representative inference; this note does not provide such variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is not an empirical ILSA/OECD assessment analysis; it is a descriptive governance country note summarizing institutional roles and expenditure allocation. Because there is no student-level cognitive outcome being scaled (e.g., no PV-based achievement scores), plausible values are not applicable. Similarly, missing-data handling is not reported because no microdata model estimation is conducted.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Austria country note describes how adult skills systems are governed across Austria’s federal, regional (nine Bundesländer), and local (2 093 municipalities) levels. It summarizes which ministries and agencies set strategy, provide intelligence, implement programmes, fund activities, and deliver services across policy areas including VET, higher VET, continuous education and training, adult education, and active labour market policies (ALMPs). The note also reports expenditure allocation shares at the subnational level (17.4% to federal states and 15.7% to local level) and explains the “combined system” governance model. No ILSA assessment instruments, sampling procedures, scaling models, or PV-based achievement outcomes are analyzed, so there are no ML model performance metrics or statistical benchmarks. The implications are therefore institutional: policy coordination and implementation capacity depend on the division of responsibilities among national ministries, regional governments, and PES branches.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the document is a descriptive governance note rather than an empirical large-scale assessment study. It does not report an analytic student sample, PV handling, missing-data strategy, or any ML modeling results; therefore fields related to predictive modeling and estimation are intentionally empty. This is consistent with a policy/administrative overview that compiles responsibilities and expenditure shares rather than estimating relationships from assessment data.
